about.title: San Bernardino Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Plenty of San Bernardino work happens on the move. Delivery drivers, service technicians, and crews traveling between job sites spend their shifts on I-215, SR-210, E Highland Avenue, and W Baseline Street, which are the corridors with the highest public-record collision counts in the city. In 2025, San Bernardino logged 1,380 injury collisions and 2,068 people injured, and reported crashes tend to cluster on Fridays between 5 p.m. and 7 p.m., right when many shifts are winding down. If you were hurt at work, California workers' compensation is usually your only remedy against your employer, and it applies no matter who was at fault. What many people miss is that a separate claim may exist against someone other than your employer: a subcontractor, the owner of the property where you were working, the maker of a tool or machine, or another driver. LawProactive is not a law firm. We connect San Bernardino County workers, at no cost, with an independent attorney who can look at both paths and explain which ones fit your situation.

items.title: Two Claims, Not One
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually your exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent subcontractor, property owner, equipment manufacturer, or another driver can be held responsible separately. An attorney in our network can tell you whether a third-party claim exists alongside your comp case.

items.title: Reporting and Retaliation Explained
items.desc: California asks you to report a work injury to your employer within 30 days, and it is illegal for an employer to punish you for doing so. The attorney we connect you with can help you understand those protections before you sign anything.

items.title: Deadlines Tracked, No Upfront Fees
items.desc: Third-party injury claims in California carry a 2-year deadline, and missing it can end the claim. Attorneys in our network work on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery, and our connection service is always free.

items.question: I was hit while driving for work on I-215 in San Bernardino. Is that a workers' comp case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It may be both. Because you were on the job, workers' compensation generally covers your medical care and part of your lost wages regardless of fault. If another driver caused the crash, you may also have a separate third-party claim against that driver. An attorney can review the collision report and explain how the two claims interact so one does not undercut the other.

items.question: Can my employer fire me for reporting an injury?
items.answer: No. Retaliation for reporting a workplace injury is illegal in California. You should still report the injury to your employer within 30 days, ideally in writing, so there is a record of when and how it happened. If you feel pressured or your hours suddenly change after reporting, mention it to the attorney you are connected with.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a claim after a San Bernardino work injury?
items.answer: The workers' comp process starts with reporting the injury to your employer within 30 days. If a third party such as a subcontractor, property owner, or equipment maker contributed to your injury, that separate claim carries a 2-year deadline under California law. Because evidence like job-site photos and equipment records can disappear quickly, it helps to talk with an attorney well before either window closes.
